title: Cancer Patients Shouldn’t Have to Cross Oceans in Search of a Cure
gist: Op-ed excerpt (Lizzi C. Lee and Jennifer Kwan, Washington Post) arguing cancer research should join AI safety on the Trump-Xi agenda: per a WHO analysis China now runs more actively recruiting oncology trials (21%) than the US (16%), yet only 18% of recruiting cancer trials span more than one country, a costly separation especially for precision oncology.

themes.theme: China overtakes US in oncology trial volume

insights.claim: A WHO analysis of 89,069 interventional cancer trials from 1999-2022 found China accounted for 21% of actively recruiting oncology studies versus 16% for the United States.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: China is now the larger source of recruiting cancer-trial evidence, relevant for biopharma pipeline sourcing and licensing from China.
insights.quote: China accounted for 21 percent of actively recruiting oncology studies, compared with 16 percent for the United States

insights.claim: Only 18% of recruiting cancer trials involve more than one country, so the US and Chinese cancer-research ecosystems produce large amounts of evidence with little overlap.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Low cross-border trial overlap means duplicated R&D cost and slower regulatory acceptance of China-generated data.
insights.quote: only 18 percent of recruiting cancer trials involved more than one country

insights.claim: The separation between US and Chinese cancer research is especially costly for precision oncology, where treatment depends on the unique DNA patterns of a patient's tumor and benefits from larger, more diverse datasets.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Precision-oncology developers face data fragmentation that cross-border collaboration could relieve.
insights.quote: That separation is costly, especially in precision oncology

themes.theme: Health as a US-China cooperation track

insights.claim: The authors argue cancer research should be added to the Trump-Xi summit agenda alongside trade, AI and national security, modeled on the separate bilateral AI safety talks that show rivals can manage shared problems together.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Signals a possible low-politics cooperation channel that could ease biotech decoupling pressure.
insights.quote: Cancer research should also be on the table.

insights.claim: The US and Chinese governments are separately conducting bilateral talks on AI safety, which the authors read as an acknowledgment that geopolitical rivals sometimes find problems worth managing together.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Existence of US-China AI safety talks is a datapoint on de-escalation channels amid tech rivalry.
insights.quote: an acknowledgment that geopolitical rivals sometimes find problems worth managing together
